title: The Video Call Body
hook: On a video call your body shrinks to a head and shoulders in a box, and everything you used to say with your whole body has to fit inside it.
why:
For many people, more working conversations now happen through a camera than across a table. Interviews, team meetings, client pitches, appraisals and even difficult conversations take place on a screen. Yet most of what this book has taught assumes two bodies in the same room: the distance between them, the angle of their shoulders, their feet, their hands, the small movements a listener makes without thinking. On a video call, almost all of that disappears or changes.

This chapter is about what happens to the body on a video call, and what to do about it. It covers what the camera keeps and what it cuts, why video calls are so tiring, how the tiny delays in the connection break the rhythm of conversation, the gaze problem that makes eye contact impossible, how to send signals a camera can carry, how to read people through a screen without over-reading, and how to design calls around human bodies rather than around the software. The next two chapters take up the camera's angle and the sound of your voice.

teach.p:
A typical video call shows a face and shoulders, cut off somewhere around the chest. Everything below is gone: the legs crossed toward or away from someone, the foot jiggling under the table, the hands folded in a lap, the lean of the whole body. Gestures made at the level of the waist vanish below the frame. A shrug becomes a small lift of the shoulders that may or may not be visible. A person's whole bearing is reduced to the angle of a head and the expression on a face.

At the same time, the face that remains is enormous. On a laptop or a large monitor, other people's faces are shown at a size that, in a room, would mean they were standing very close to you. The chapter on proxemics described how distance carries meaning and how people adjust it to manage intimacy. A video call removes that control. Every face is close, and stays close, whatever the relationship.

The result is a strange mixture of too little and too much. You lose most of the body, so the signals you relied on in a room are missing. And the face is magnified, so every flicker of the eyes and every frown is on display, both yours and theirs.

For a reader, the first lesson is humility. Readings that would be reasonable in a room may be unreliable on a screen, because the evidence is thinner. The figure here sits at a laptop in profile, upright and engaged. From the camera's point of view, almost all of this posture is invisible. Only the head and shoulders make it through, and they must carry what the whole body used to say.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if video calls carried as much nonverbal information as face-to-face meetings. The framing of a typical call makes that impossible, though higher cameras, wider shots and larger screens can restore some of what is lost.
teach.pullQuote: Readings that would be reasonable in a room may be unreliable on a screen, because the evidence is thinner.

teach.p:
Many people noticed during the pandemic that a day of video calls left them more drained than a day of meetings in person. In 2021 Jeremy Bailenson, who studies virtual communication at Stanford, set out four reasons. First, close-up eye gaze: on a call, everyone appears to be looking straight at you at close range, all the time, which in ordinary life happens only in moments of intimacy or confrontation. Second, cognitive load: in a room, sending and reading nonverbal signals happens largely without effort, while on a call people have to work at both. Third, the mirror: most software shows you your own face throughout, which no ordinary conversation does. Fourth, immobility: to stay in frame, people sit still for hours.

In a survey of more than ten thousand people, Géraldine Fauville, Bailenson and their colleagues found that women reported more fatigue from video calls than men, and that the difference was partly explained by greater anxiety about their own image on screen. Women also reported longer meetings and shorter breaks between them.

These were surveys and theoretical arguments rather than experiments, but the mechanisms suggest simple remedies. Hide your self-view once you have checked your frame. Make other people's video smaller, or use speaker view rather than a grid of faces. Take breaks between calls. Turn cameras off for some meetings, and stand or walk during audio-only ones.

The figure here has slumped at the laptop, shoulders rounded, an hour into a long call. On camera it reads as boredom. Much more often, it is simply fatigue.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if video calls were no more tiring than meetings in person. Fatigue surveys consistently find otherwise, though they rely on self-report and cannot isolate which of Bailenson's mechanisms matters most.

teach.p:
In ordinary conversation, people take turns with remarkable precision. The gap between one person finishing and the next starting is usually a fraction of a second, and speakers rely on that rhythm to know when to come in and when to hold back. Video calls break it.

In 2022 Julie Boland and her colleagues compared the same pairs of people talking face to face and over Zoom. Face to face, the average gap between turns was about 135 milliseconds. Over Zoom, it was about 487 milliseconds, more than three times as long, even though the technical delay in the connection was only a fraction of that. People also held the floor for longer on Zoom, and there were fewer changes of speaker. The researchers suggested that small, variable delays disrupt the automatic timing that normally keeps a conversation in step.

The consequences are familiar. Two people start speaking at once, both stop, both apologise, and both start again. Someone pauses to let others in, and nobody comes in. A colleague takes a beat to answer, and it feels like reluctance. Quiet people stop trying to get a word in at all.

So read pauses on a call generously. A slow answer is often the connection, not the person. If you are chairing, make turn-taking explicit: name the next speaker, use raised hands, and leave a beat longer than feels natural before moving on. The figure here sits with a hand to his face, apparently hesitating. On a call, he may simply be waiting for a gap that the technology never gives him.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if turn-taking over video were as quick and smooth as face to face. Boland and colleagues found large delays, though in one platform and one set of studies, and newer technology may narrow the gap.

teach.p:
On a call, eye contact is impossible in a strict sense. If you look at the other person's face on your screen, your camera, usually above the screen, records you looking slightly down, and to them you seem to be looking at their chest or your keyboard. If you look into the camera, they see you looking straight at them, but you can no longer see their face at all.

The chapter on gaze described how people look away while thinking and look back to check how they are being received. On a call, the looking away is still visible, and often magnified. Someone glancing at another window, reading notes or checking a message appears to be looking off into space. Someone looking down at their own face in the corner of the screen appears distracted.

There is no perfect solution, but some habits help. Place the window showing the person you are speaking with as close to the camera as possible, so that the angle is small. Look into the camera when you make a point that matters, or when you are listening to something serious, so that the other person feels addressed. Look at faces the rest of the time, to read their reactions. Tell people if you are taking notes: “I'm looking down because I'm writing this down.”

The figure here looks down and away. In a room, this is often thinking. On a screen, it can look like inattention, and the person on the other end cannot see what you are looking at. Say so when it matters.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if people on video calls read a downward gaze as attention rather than distraction. The geometry of camera and screen makes misreading likely, though people who use video calls often may learn to discount it.

teach.h: Make your signals bigger, and clearer.
teach.p:
Because the camera carries less, the small signals that keep a conversation going need a little help. The chapter on the head nod described the back channel: the nods, mm-hms and small sounds that tell a speaker you are following. On a call, these are easily lost. A small nod is barely visible in a compressed video, and the mm-hm is often cut off by noise suppression or muted microphones.

So nod a little more clearly, and let your face react. Smile when something is funny. Show surprise when something surprises you. Raise your eyebrows, tilt your head. This is not performing; it is translating your ordinary reactions into a size the medium can carry. Many people find that the video call version of themselves looks flatter than they feel, and a little extra expression simply restores the balance.

Bring your hands into the frame when you gesture, so that they can be seen. Sit far enough back that your shoulders and upper chest are visible, which lets posture carry some meaning again. Lean in slightly to show interest, but not so far that your face fills the screen.

Use the software's signals sparingly but deliberately: a thumbs-up reaction to agree without interrupting, a raised hand to ask for the floor, a short message in the chat to say you are following. The figure here is at the bottom of a nod. On a call, this movement is one of the most useful things a listener can do, and it needs to be large enough to survive the journey.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if ordinary-sized nods and expressions came across on video as clearly as in person. The reduced size and quality of video images make that unlikely, though the right amount of extra expression varies with the person and the setting.

teach.p:
Reading on a call needs extra care, because the evidence is thinner and the rivals are more numerous. A frozen face may be a frozen connection. A delay may be latency. A sudden glance away may be a child entering the room, a message arriving or a second screen. A flat expression may be fatigue, poor lighting or a camera that makes everyone look grey.

Cameras switched off deserve particular generosity. People turn their cameras off because of slow connections, shared or untidy homes, a crying baby, exhaustion, anxiety about their appearance, a disability or because watching faces all day is overwhelming, which is true for many neurodivergent people. Treating a camera that is off as a sign of disengagement is usually unfair.

Use the channels you have. The voice, which the next chapter but one examines, carries a great deal on a call. Listen for changes in pace and tone. Notice who speaks and who stays silent, and who tries to speak and gives up. Read the chat as well as the faces. And build a baseline for each person on video, because their video self may differ from their in-person self.

When something matters, check. “You've gone quiet; are you still with us?” or “I can't read your face on this connection; what do you think?” The figure here sits back with arms folded. In a room, the posture might say something. On a call, it may just be the way he sits when he cannot see anyone's body either.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if readings made through video were as reliable as readings made in person. Fewer channels and more rivals make them less reliable, though some signals, such as voice, survive well.

teach.p:
Much of the strain of video calls comes from habits that could be changed. Back-to-back meetings with no breaks, cameras required for every call, hour-long slots for twenty minutes of business and grids of twenty faces are choices, not laws of nature.

If you run meetings, you can change them. Make meetings shorter, and leave gaps between them. Make cameras optional for some calls, and model it yourself. Use audio-only calls for one-to-one conversations where faces add little, and suggest walking while you talk. The opening chapter of Part III described how many men talk most easily side by side; a walking phone call has some of the same quality, with neither person watching the other's face.

Think about which conversations need the face. A difficult conversation, a piece of bad news or an apology may be better in person if possible, or on a call with cameras on and full attention. Routine updates may be better as a message. Matching the medium to the conversation is part of reading people well.

And look after your own body. Stand up between calls. Look into the distance. Move. The figure here walks while on the phone. For many conversations, this is a better arrangement than two faces frozen in boxes, and both people often end the call less tired than they began it.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if shorter meetings, optional cameras and audio-only calls made no difference to fatigue. Research on video fatigue points to these factors, though direct trials of meeting design are few.

poseGallery.doCaption: Seated back, at a comfortable distance
poseGallery.annotation: A face pushed toward the camera appears at the distance of a whisper. Sitting back lets your shoulders, posture and hands back into the picture.

poseGallery.doCaption: A walking call with the camera off
poseGallery.dontCaption: Slumped in front of a camera for an hour
poseGallery.annotation: Not every conversation needs faces. Audio-only calls, especially on the move, remove the mirror and the stare and often go better.

poseGallery.doCaption: Clear nods the camera can carry
poseGallery.annotation: On a call, small signals are lost. A clearer nod and a visible reaction tell the speaker you are with them.

poseGallery.doCaption: Looking into the camera for the key point
poseGallery.dontCaption: Appearing to look down at the keyboard
poseGallery.annotation: Faces on the screen sit below the camera. Look at them to read, and into the lens for the moments that matter.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Headphones on, half in another window
poseGallery.annotation: On a call it is easy to drift into email, and people can often tell from your eyes. Close the other windows for the conversations that count.

caseStudy:
Owen, forty-five, manages a team of engineers spread across three cities. Since his company went remote, he spends six or seven hours a day on video calls. He ends each day exhausted and short-tempered, and in his annual review, two of his team say that he comes across as cold and distracted in meetings.

Owen is hurt and puzzled, so he watches a recording of one of his calls, as the chapter on video review suggested. He sees what they see. His laptop sits low on the desk, so he looks down at the camera. He spends half of each call looking at the corner of the screen where his own face is. His reactions are tiny, a flicker of the eyebrows that the camera barely records. When people pause for him to come in, he waits, and the pause stretches until someone else fills it.

He makes a few changes. He hides his self-view after the first minute. He raises the laptop on a stack of books and moves the speaker's window up near the camera. He cuts meetings to twenty-five minutes, so there are gaps between them, and makes cameras optional for the daily update. When he chairs, he names the next speaker and leaves a longer pause before moving on. He lets his face react, and nods so that it shows. Once a week, he and his deputy have their one-to-one as a phone call while both of them walk.

Three months later, the team's comments are different. One engineer says that Owen seems more relaxed. Owen says that he is less tired than he has been in two years, and that the walking calls are the best conversations of his week.
observe: On your next call, notice how much of each person's body you can see, and what you are relying on to read them.
Notice how often people talk over each other or leave long gaps, and how the group recovers.
Notice where your own eyes go during a call: faces, your own image, notes, other windows.
Notice who turns their camera off and when, and resist the first explanation that comes to mind.

drills.name: Watch Yourself Once
steps: Record five minutes of a real or practice video call, with permission from anyone else on it.
Watch it with the sound off, and note what your face, head and shoulders say.
Note where your eyes go, and how often you look at your own image.
Note how visible your nods and reactions are.
Write down two changes you will make, and try them on your next call.
variations: Record a short call with your camera at two different heights, and compare how your gaze appears in each.
Watch a recorded call with the sound on and then off, and note which signals carry better without audio.

drills.name: Fix the Frame
steps: Raise your camera so that the lens is roughly at eye level.
Sit back until your shoulders and upper chest are in the frame.
Move the window showing the speaker as close to the camera as you can.
Turn off your self-view once you have checked how you look.
variations: Try your setup with a window in front of you and then behind you, and compare how readable your face is.
Ask a colleague to tell you honestly how you look on their screen, and adjust one thing they mention.

drills.name: Chair for the Delay
steps: In the next meeting you run, name the person you want to hear from next instead of asking the room.
Leave a pause of three full seconds before moving on from a question.
Ask quieter people directly, by name, for their view.
Afterwards, note who spoke who usually does not.
variations: Try ending one meeting five minutes early, and notice how people use the time and how they respond.
In a meeting you run, ask everyone to use a hand signal when they want to speak, and see whether talking over each other drops.

drills.name: Walk One Call
steps: Choose one one-to-one conversation this week that does not need faces or a screen.
Suggest doing it as a phone call while both of you walk.
Notice how the conversation differs from your usual video calls.
Ask the other person afterwards how it felt for them.
variations: Try the walking call with someone you usually only see on video, and compare the conversations.
Suggest an audio-only call for a meeting that usually has cameras, and ask people afterwards how it felt.

quiz.q: A colleague says that a video call is just a meeting on a screen, so all the same body language rules apply. What does this chapter suggest?
options: He is right; cameras capture everything a meeting room shows
Video cuts most of the body, magnifies faces and adds new strains
Video calls carry more nonverbal information than meetings in person
Body language plays no part in video calls, so it can be ignored
quiz.explain: A typical frame shows only head and shoulders, faces appear at intimate size, and Bailenson identified close-up gaze, cognitive load, the mirror and immobility as sources of strain. Readings that are reasonable in a room may be unreliable on screen.

quiz.q: What did Fauville, Bailenson and colleagues find about who reports more fatigue from video calls?
options: Men reported far more fatigue, because they are less used to cameras
Fatigue was the same for everyone once meeting length was considered
Women reported more fatigue, partly linked to anxiety about self-view
Only people over sixty reported any fatigue from video calls at all
quiz.explain: Women reported more fatigue, and the difference was partly explained by anxiety about their own image on screen. Women also reported longer meetings and shorter breaks, which suggests simple remedies.

quiz.q: What did Boland and colleagues find when the same pairs of people talked face to face and over Zoom?
options: The gaps between turns were more than three times longer over Zoom
Turn-taking was faster over Zoom because people were paying closer attention
There was no difference in the rhythm of conversation at all
People changed speakers more often over Zoom than face to face
quiz.explain: Turn transitions averaged about 135 milliseconds face to face and about 487 over Zoom, far more than the technical delay. People also held the floor longer, with fewer changes of speaker.

quiz.q: On a video call, a colleague takes a noticeable beat before answering your question. What fits this chapter best?
options: Treat it as reluctance and ask him what he is really unhappy about
Treat it as a sign that he does not know the answer to the question
Repeat the question more loudly, since he probably did not hear it
Remember that delays disrupt timing on calls, and wait for his answer
quiz.explain: Small delays on calls greatly slow turn-taking, so a pause is often the connection rather than the person. Reading it as reluctance or ignorance adds a story the evidence does not support.

quiz.q: Why does looking at someone's face on your screen often make you appear to be looking down?
options: Because screens make everyone look tired, whatever they are doing
Because the camera usually sits above the screen, not where the face is
Because people instinctively lower their heads during video calls
Because video compression shifts the apparent position of the eyes on the screen
quiz.explain: The camera records you from above the screen, so looking at the image below it reads as looking down. Placing the speaker's window near the camera, and looking into the lens for important points, reduces the problem.

quiz.q: After six hours of back-to-back video calls, you feel drained and irritable. What does this chapter suggest?
options: Push through, since video fatigue is just a matter of willpower
Turn your self-view on, so you can check you look more engaged
Hide self-view, take breaks, and move some calls to audio or walking
Lengthen each call so that you can cover everything in fewer meetings
quiz.explain: The mirror, the stare and immobility all add strain. Hiding self-view, building in breaks and moving suitable conversations to audio-only or walking calls address the mechanisms directly.

quiz.q: Which of these is one of the four causes of video call fatigue that Bailenson proposed?
options: Seeing your own face in the self-view window for hours
The cost of electricity used by the computer during long calls
Sitting further from other people than you normally would in a room
Hearing other people's voices more loudly and clearly than in person
quiz.explain: Bailenson's four causes were close-up eye gaze, cognitive load, the mirror of seeing your own face, and reduced mobility. Hiding self-view is one of the simplest ways to reduce the strain.

quiz.q: A capable team member almost always keeps his camera off in team meetings, and colleagues have started joking about it. What fits this chapter best?
options: Make cameras compulsory for everyone, so that nobody can hide
Join in the joke, so that he understands how his absence looks
Ask him privately and kindly, since there are many ordinary reasons
Assume he is doing other work, and give him less important tasks
quiz.explain: Cameras go off for many reasons, from shared homes to mirror anxiety. Asking privately and offering options respects him, and judging him by his contributions rather than his video is fairer.

quiz.q: Someone says that a candidate who looks down throughout a video interview is avoiding eye contact. What does this chapter say?
options: It is right, since confident candidates always look straight into the camera
She is probably looking at faces on her screen, below the camera
It is right, but only if she also speaks quietly and hesitates often
It is wrong, since gaze tells you nothing at all on any video call
quiz.explain: Looking at someone's face on a screen makes you appear to look down, because the camera is above it. Reading that as evasion puts a judgment on a piece of equipment.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific video call in the past week that went less well than you hoped, or that left you particularly tired. Describe your setup: camera height, where you looked, whether your self-view was on, how much of your body was in frame. How did the rhythm of turn-taking go? What did you read in other people's faces or silences, and how confident should you have been? Write two changes you will make to your setup and one to how you read others on screen.
reflection.guidance: Be practical and concrete: the height of the laptop, the window you watched, the pause you misread. If you can, watch a recording of yourself before writing. The aim is not perfection on camera but a setup that tires you less and lets your ordinary warmth and attention come through.

failureMode: The first failure is to read people on video as if they were in the room, drawing confident conclusions from a face that is compressed, delayed and missing most of its body. The second is to treat delays and pauses as reluctance, coldness or ignorance, when the connection is often to blame. The third is to stare at your own image, look down at a low camera and keep your reactions so small that the camera loses them, and then wonder why people find you cold. The fourth is to treat cameras that are off as disengagement without considering the many reasons people switch them off. And the fifth is to accept a day of back-to-back calls as normal, rather than shortening meetings, adding breaks and moving the right conversations to audio or a walk.

moreCases.title: The candidate who would not look up
moreCases.scene:
Sana, twenty-eight, is interviewing by video for a job as a data analyst. She is sitting at her kitchen table with her laptop flat in front of her. The camera is at the top of the screen, well below her eye level, and she looks down at the interviewers' faces on the screen throughout. To the three people on the panel, she appears to be looking at her keyboard, or her lap, for the whole forty minutes.

Her answers are strong: clear, detailed and well structured. But afterwards, one of the panel, Gareth, says that she did not make eye contact once, and that he is not sure she would be confident with clients. Another says she seemed nervous. The third, Helen, says that Sana was looking at their faces on her screen, which is exactly what anyone would do, and that they all look the same way to her.

Gareth says that confident people look at the camera.

Sana had practised her answers with a friend over video the night before, and the friend had said she looked great. Neither of them had noticed the camera angle, because they were looking at each other's faces on the screen.

Gareth has interviewed dozens of people in person and has a strong sense of what confidence looks like across a table. He has interviewed only a handful by video, and has not adjusted his sense of it.
moreCases.misread:
Gareth read Sana's downward gaze as a lack of eye contact, and from that as a lack of confidence, as he would have in a room. He did not account for the camera, which records anyone looking at faces on a screen as looking slightly down.

He also read his own preference, for people who look into the camera, as a measure of confidence, when it is mostly a measure of whether someone has learned a technique.

And the panel did not mention, in their discussion, that all three of them had looked down at their screens in exactly the same way. The camera that made Sana look evasive made them look the same to her.

Sana, for her part, had no idea how she looked. Without a self-view she had checked, she could not see the problem, which is exactly why the reader on the other side needs to allow for it.
moreCases.betterRead:
On a call, eye contact in the strict sense is impossible. If you look at the other person's face on your screen, the camera above it records you looking down; if you look into the camera, you can no longer see them. Sana was doing what almost everyone does on video: looking at the people she was talking to. A low laptop exaggerated the effect. Reading her gaze as it would be read in a room put a judgment on a piece of equipment. Helen's better reading kept the panel's attention on what the interview could measure, the answers, and on the fact that all three of them looked the same on Sana's screen. Gareth agreed to score the answers first. Sana was offered the job. In her first week, Helen mentioned, kindly, that a pile of books under the laptop would raise the camera, and Sana laughed and said she had wondered why everyone always seemed to be looking at her chin.

Gareth also asked, at the next panel, whether they could agree in advance what they would and would not read from video.

moreCases.title: The colleague whose camera was always off
moreCases.scene:
Mark manages a team of eight who work remotely. Most of them keep their cameras on in team meetings. One, Tom, twenty-six, almost always keeps his off. He speaks when asked, his contributions are useful, and his work is good. But Mark has started to feel that Tom is not really present, and wonders whether he is doing other work during meetings, or does not care. Two other team members have made jokes about Tom being the "invisible man".

Mark considers making cameras compulsory for all team meetings. He mentions this to a colleague in another department, who asks whether he has asked Tom why.

He has not.

Tom also messages Mark after most meetings with useful thoughts he did not raise in the meeting itself. Mark has found these helpful, and has not connected them with the camera.

Mark has noticed that he feels more connected to the people whose faces he can see, and that he tends to address his questions to them. Tom, with no face on the screen, gets asked less, and so says less, which has made Mark more convinced that he is not engaged. Mark has not noticed the loop.

Tom, for his part, has noticed that he is the only one with his camera off, and has started to feel that it is being held against him. He has thought about saying something, and decided it would sound like an excuse.
moreCases.misread:
Mark read Tom's camera being off as a sign of disengagement, and the jokes from colleagues as confirmation. He was about to set a rule for everyone on the strength of a reading he had not checked.

The colleagues' jokes also changed how Mark saw Tom. A joke repeated in a group can turn an ordinary behaviour into a reputation, without anyone having checked whether it was fair.

He also nearly turned a reading about one person into a rule for eight, which is how unchecked readings tend to grow in teams.

The questions Mark asked, mostly to visible faces, were a small but steady signal to Tom that he was less part of the team.
moreCases.betterRead:
People turn their cameras off for many reasons: slow connections, shared or untidy homes, a crying baby, exhaustion, anxiety about being watched, a disability, or simply finding the constant self-view tiring. Bailenson's account of video call fatigue included mirror anxiety, the strain of seeing your own face for hours, and Fauville and colleagues found that this mirror anxiety was linked to how tired people felt. A camera that is off says nothing reliable about attention. Mark's better approach was to ask, privately and kindly. In a one-to-one, he said, "I notice your camera's usually off in team meetings. That's fine, I'm just curious whether there's anything I could do to make calls easier for you." Tom said that he shared a flat with three people, worked from his bedroom and was embarrassed by it, and that his connection was poor. Mark arranged a company headset and a virtual background, said that cameras would be optional for team meetings, and asked the team to drop the joke. Tom started switching his camera on for one-to-ones, which was what Mark had really wanted.

Mark also stopped judging people's attention by their camera, and started noticing who followed up and who did not.

moreCases.title: The argument across the time zones
moreCases.scene:
Leah, thirty, is living in Melbourne for a year on a work placement. Her partner, Jake, is in London. They talk on video every evening for her and every morning for him. Recently the calls have become tense. When Leah is telling Jake something, he often starts talking just as she continues, and they end up talking over each other, both stopping and both saying "Sorry, go on." When Jake answers a question, there is a pause, and Leah reads it as hesitation. Last week, when she asked whether he missed her, the pause before his "Of course" felt like a lifetime.

Leah starts to wonder whether Jake is losing interest. Jake starts to feel that Leah is impatient and always interrupting him.

On one call, the connection freezes for several seconds while Jake is in the middle of telling her about his week, and when it comes back, Leah has missed the end of his sentence and he is waiting for a reply.

Leah's flat in Melbourne has a poor internet connection, and Jake usually calls from the train on his way to work. Neither of them has ever thought about how much the setting was adding to the strain.

They have also started to dread the calls a little, which neither has admitted. Leah notices that she checks her hair in the self-view before Jake answers, and Jake notices that he has started to keep them shorter.
moreCases.misread:
Leah read Jake's pauses as hesitation and his talking over her as not listening. Jake read Leah's interruptions as impatience. Both read the broken rhythm of the call as information about the other person's feelings.

They also both read the apologies, "Sorry, go on", as signs of tension, when they were the ordinary sound of two people working round a delay.

They also read their own frustration with the technology as frustration with each other, which is one of the most common and least noticed ways that video strains a relationship.
moreCases.betterRead:
Boland and colleagues found that the gap between turns in conversation was more than three times as long over Zoom as face to face, and a connection between Melbourne and London is likely to add further delay. The rhythm people rely on to know when to speak is broken, so they talk over each other, apologise and wait too long, and every pause feels heavier than it is. Leah's reading of the pause before "Of course" was a reading of the connection, not of Jake. The better approach was to name the lag and adjust for it. They agreed to leave a beat after each other finished, to use a small hand signal when one of them wanted to speak, and to say important things on a voice message if the connection was bad, so that the words arrived whole. Leah also asked, at the end of a call, "Your pause before 'Of course' worried me. Was that the lag?" Jake laughed and said he had been yawning, which was a different problem.

They also switched to audio-only calls when the connection was bad, and found that they talked over each other less.

moreCases.title: The appraisal on a frozen screen
moreCases.scene:
Dev, thirty-eight, is giving a team member, Rachel, a difficult appraisal by video. He tells her that her project has missed its deadlines twice and that the client has complained. As he says it, Rachel's image freezes: her face is caught with her mouth slightly open and her eyes wide. The audio continues for a moment, then cuts out. Dev waits. After about ten seconds, the picture jerks back to life. Rachel is now looking down, her face flat.

Dev reads the frozen face as shock and the flat face as defiance. He becomes firmer, and starts going through the complaints in detail. Rachel says very little for the rest of the call. At the end, she says, quietly, that she missed some of what he said because her connection dropped.

Dev realises that he does not know which parts she heard.

Rachel is working from her parents' house that week, because her own flat has a leak, and the broadband there is unreliable. She mentioned this to Dev at the start of the call, but he did not register it.

Dev has prepared the conversation carefully, with notes on the deadlines and a copy of the client's email open on his second screen. He glances at the notes several times as he speaks, which on Rachel's screen looks as though he is looking away from her.
moreCases.misread:
Dev read Rachel's frozen expression as a reaction to his words, and her face when the picture returned as defiance. He did not consider that he was reading a frozen frame and a moment of recovery from a dropped connection.

He also became firmer in response to his reading, which is how a misread face on video can turn a difficult conversation into a harder one.

He also read Rachel's silence for the rest of the call as sullenness, when she may simply have been trying to work out what she had missed.

And his own glances at his notes, which Rachel could see, may have looked to her like a man reading a script rather than talking to her, which would not have helped either.
moreCases.betterRead: Reading on a call needs extra care because the evidence is thinner and the rivals are more numerous. A frozen face may be a frozen connection. A delay may be latency. A flat face may be poor lighting, fatigue or someone trying to work out what they missed. Dev's sequence of readings, shock and then defiance, may have been accurate, or may have been entirely about the technology, and he had no way of telling. The better approach, especially for difficult news, is to check in words and to make the important points robust to a bad connection. Dev rang Rachel that afternoon, on the phone, and said he was sorry the call had been patchy. He went through the main points again, slowly, and asked what she had heard and what she thought. Rachel said that she knew about the deadlines and had been waiting for a chance to explain that two of her team had been off sick. They agreed a plan, and Dev sent a short written summary afterwards, so that nothing depended on a single dropped call.

workedReading.title: A hard conversation on video
workedReading.scene:
Nadia manages a team spread across three offices. She needs to tell one of her senior engineers, Simon, that a reorganisation will move him onto a different project, one he has said before that he does not want. They are in different cities, and a video call is the only option this week. Nadia knows that Simon is proud of his current work and that the news will be unwelcome. She also knows how much a video call takes away.

She also knows that Simon is more relaxed on the phone than on video, and that he tends to switch his camera off when calls are tense. She decides to let him choose, and to make the call as easy for him as she can.

Nadia also knows that she will not be able to see Simon's hands, his feet, or whether he turns away from the desk. Whatever he feels, most of his body will be telling it to an empty room.

She also reminds herself that Simon will remember how this call felt long after he has forgotten the details, and that the care she takes now is part of the message.

steps.label: Set the frame before the call
steps.text:
Nadia raises her laptop on a stack of books so that the camera is at eye level, sits back so that her shoulders and upper chest are in the frame, and sits facing a window so that her face is evenly lit. She moves the window showing Simon to just below the camera, and turns off her own self-view once she has checked it, so that she will not spend the call watching herself.

She also closes her email and silences notifications, so that nothing flashes on her screen while she is talking. A glance at a notification, on video, looks like a glance away from the person.

She also checks the background behind her. A cluttered room or a busy office can distract on video in a way it would not in person, because it fills so much of the small picture.

She also puts a glass of water within reach, out of shot, so that she will not have to leave the frame or reach awkwardly if her mouth goes dry.

steps.label: Give him notice and a choice
steps.text:
She sends Simon a short message beforehand: she would like to talk about the reorganisation, it may not be what he hopes, and would he prefer video or a phone call. He replies video. Giving notice and a choice of medium restores a little of the control that a screen takes away.

She also books the call for a time when he will have the rest of the afternoon free, so that he does not have to go straight into another meeting after hearing difficult news.

She also tells him in the message that the conversation will take about half an hour, so that he can plan around it and does not have to wonder how long it will last.

steps.label: Say the hard part early
steps.text:
She does not bury the news. After a brief hello, she says, slowly, looking into the camera for the key sentence, "I want to tell you about the reorganisation. You're going to be moving onto the payments project from next month." Looking into the camera at that moment means that, on Simon's screen, she is looking straight at him when it matters.

She also says it in one clear sentence, without a long preamble. On video, a long build-up can feel even more anxious than in person, because the other person cannot read the room around the words.

She also avoids softening it so much that the message is lost. On video, where reactions are harder to read, clarity is a kindness: Simon should not be left wondering what she meant.

steps.label: Leave room for the lag
steps.text:
Then she stops, and waits, for longer than she would in a room. She knows that pauses on video are longer than they feel, and that if she fills the silence she may talk over his first reaction. After about three seconds, Simon says, "Right," and nothing else. His face is still and his shoulders have lifted.

She also keeps her own face still and warm while she waits, rather than looking away or checking her notes. On his screen, her face is the only thing in the room.

She also keeps her hands visible, just in the frame, resting on the desk. Hands that disappear below the frame can look as though someone is doing something else.

steps.label: Read what the camera carries
steps.text:
With most of his body out of frame, Nadia reads what she can: the raised shoulders, the jaw set, his gaze dropping off the screen, his voice flatter than usual. She reminds herself that the picture is compressed and the light in his room is poor, and that any single sign may be the camera. Together, they fit a man taking a blow and trying not to show it.

She also notices that he has turned slightly away from the camera, so that she can see more of the side of his face. People on video often turn a little away when they want privacy, as they would turn away in a room.

She also notices that his microphone has picked up a sharp breath out, which the camera might not have shown. On video, the audio often carries signals the picture loses.

steps.label: Check in words
steps.text:
She does not guess. She says, "I know this isn't what you wanted. How are you feeling about it?" and waits again. Simon says that he is disappointed and that he feels as if his work on the current project has not been valued. Nadia listens, nods clearly enough for the camera to carry it, and says that his work has been valued, and why he was chosen for the new project.

She also uses his name when she reassures him, and looks into the camera as she does it. Small moments of direct gaze carry more weight on video, because they are rarer.

She also asks him whether there is anything he would like her to pass on to the directors, which gives him a way to influence the decision rather than only receive it.

steps.label: Follow up off the screen
steps.text:
She ends by saying that she knows video makes these conversations harder, and offers to talk again on the phone the next day, once he has had time to think. She sends a short written summary afterwards. The next day, on the phone, Simon asks several practical questions and says he is coming round to it. Nadia notes that the call had taken away his body, his room and half a second of every reply, and that each step she took had been a way of giving a little of that back.

She also thanks him, in the written summary, for how he took the news. A short note of thanks after a hard call helps the other person feel that the relationship survived it.

She also notes that she would have handled it differently in person: a walk, a coffee, more time. Video asked her to do everything a little more deliberately, and that turned out to be no bad thing.

moreFailures.title: Reading people on video as if they were in the room
moreFailures.body:
The temptation on a call is to read a face as confidently as you would across a table: a frown means disagreement, a downward gaze means evasion, a still face means coldness. But the face on a screen is compressed, delayed, lit badly and cut off at the chest, and the person may be looking at you, at themselves, at a second screen or at a child who has just walked in. Most of their body, which would normally help you weigh a facial expression, is gone. Read video faces more lightly than real ones, look for clusters across the whole call rather than single moments, and check important readings in words.

It also helps to remember that people adjust their faces for the camera in ways they would not in a room. Some freeze, some over-smile, some go blank. What you see on video may be partly a performance for the lens.

It also helps to watch for the moments when the picture and the sound disagree. A face that seems calm with a voice that has gone tight is often a better clue than either alone.

It also helps to know that video compresses faces in ways that remove subtle movements first: the small changes around the eyes, the flicker of a smile. What survives is often the larger, more deliberate expression, which may not be the most honest one.

moreFailures.title: Treating delays as reluctance
moreFailures.body:
Boland and colleagues found that the gap between turns was about three times as long over Zoom as face to face. A pause that would mean hesitation in a room may mean nothing at all on a call, and a reply that seems to come late may have been spoken on time. People also talk over each other more, because the rhythm that tells them when to speak is broken. Do not read pauses as reluctance, coldness or ignorance on a call. Leave longer gaps yourself, name people when you want them to speak, and when a pause worries you, ask about it rather than deciding what it meant.

It also helps to say, at the start of an important call, that you know there may be lag, and to agree how you will handle it. It makes pauses easier to bear for both of you.

It also helps to watch for who gets talked over most on calls. Quieter people, junior colleagues and people with slower connections often lose their turn repeatedly, and a chair who notices can give it back.

It also helps to watch for the pattern of who speaks first after a question. On video, the most confident or best-connected person often answers before anyone else has had a chance, and others give up waiting.

It also helps to repeat key decisions at the end of a call, so that anyone who lost a few seconds to the connection still leaves knowing what was agreed.

moreFailures.title: Watching yourself instead of them
moreFailures.body:
Most video software shows you your own face throughout the call, and many people spend a surprising share of every call looking at it. Bailenson described this mirror as one of the four causes of video call fatigue, and it also takes your attention away from the person you are talking to, which they can often see in your eyes. Check your frame at the start, and then hide your self-view. Move the window showing the other person as close to your camera as you can, so that your gaze looks more natural to them, and give them the attention you would in a room.

It also helps to notice when you are checking how you look rather than how they are. If your eyes keep drifting to your own image, that is a sign to hide it.

It also helps to place the window of the person you are talking to near the camera, rather than across the screen. The closer their face is to the lens, the more your gaze will look like eye contact to them.

It also helps to know that many people feel more self-conscious on video than in person, partly because of the self-view. Hiding it often makes people more natural, and so easier to read.

moreFailures.title: Reading a camera that is off as disengagement
moreFailures.body:
A camera that is off is easy to read as absence, boredom or doing something else. Often it is none of these. People turn cameras off because of poor connections, shared homes, children, disability, exhaustion, anxiety, or because they listen better without seeing themselves. Treating camera-off as a failing, through jokes, comments or a rule that cameras must always be on, can make people more anxious and less willing to speak. If it matters, ask privately and kindly, and offer options. Judge engagement by what people contribute, not by whether their face is on the screen.

It also helps to remember that people with disabilities, including some autistic people and people with chronic illness, may find cameras particularly draining. Optional cameras are an accessibility measure as well as a courtesy.

It also helps to be clear about expectations. If cameras are needed for a particular call, such as a client meeting, say so in advance, and say why, so that people can prepare rather than feel caught out.

And remember that camera-off can also be a sign that something is wrong, such as illness or a crisis at home. If someone who usually has their camera on suddenly switches it off for weeks, a kind, private question is worth asking.

questions.q: Why do video calls make me so tired?
questions.a:
Bailenson proposed four reasons. Close-up eye gaze: on a call, faces appear large and close, as if everyone were staring at you from intimate distance, all the time. Cognitive load: sending and reading signals takes conscious effort on video, because so many of them are missing or delayed. The mirror: seeing your own face for hours is unusual and tiring. Reduced mobility: you are stuck in a small space in front of a camera, unable to move as you would in a room. Fauville and colleagues developed a scale to measure the fatigue and found it widespread. Shorter calls, breaks between them, hiding self-view and allowing audio-only calls all help.

It also helps to stand up and move between calls, even for a minute or two, and to look at something far away. The body and eyes recover faster with small breaks than with none.

It also helps to switch to speaker view rather than a grid for most of a call. A single face is less tiring to watch than a wall of faces, all apparently looking at you at once.

And it helps to remember that video fatigue is not a personal weakness. It is a predictable effect of a medium that asks the body to do unusual things for long periods.

questions.q: Should I look at the camera or at the screen?
questions.a:
Both, at different moments. Looking at the other person's face on your screen lets you read them, but makes you appear to be looking slightly down. Looking into the camera makes you appear to look straight at them, but means you cannot see their reaction. A practical compromise is to look at their face most of the time, and to look into the camera for the moments that matter most: a greeting, a key point, an important question, a thank you. Moving their window as close to the camera as possible reduces the gap between the two.

It also helps to tell people what you are doing. "I'm looking at my notes" or "I'm looking at your slides" explains a glance away that might otherwise be misread.

It also helps to look into the camera when you are listening to something important, as well as when you are speaking. It tells the speaker that you are paying attention, which a downward gaze can hide.

It also helps to practise. Recording yourself for a minute while looking at the screen and then at the camera shows the difference clearly, and makes it easier to choose when to do each.

questions.q: Is it rude to turn my camera off?
questions.a:
It depends on the setting and the norms of the group, and it is worth thinking about how others will read it. In some teams, cameras off is normal; in others, it can look as though you are not engaged. If you need to turn it off, a short explanation helps: "My connection's poor today, so I'll keep my camera off," or "I listen better without the video." For one-to-one conversations and anything sensitive, having your camera on, if you can, usually helps the other person read you. If you run meetings, making cameras optional for some calls is one of the simplest ways to reduce fatigue.

It also helps to switch on for the start and end of a call, even if you turn the camera off in the middle. A face at the greeting and goodbye carries much of the warmth that the rest of the call might lack.

It also helps to keep your microphone on mute when you are not speaking, so that background noise does not distract, and to unmute clearly when you want to come in.

If you are new to a team, it helps to watch what others do for the first few calls, and to ask your manager what is expected.

questions.q: How can I read someone whose camera is off?
questions.a:
Through the voice and the words, as you would on the phone. Listen to their pace, pitch and volume, the pauses before their answers, and where their voice drops, as the chapter on audio as body language describes. Notice what they say and what they leave out. Notice whether they contribute, ask questions and follow up, which tell you more about engagement than a face would. Because you have less to go on, check important readings in words: "You sounded unsure about that. What do you think?" And be generous: missing video is not missing attention.

It also helps to say more aloud than you would in person, such as "That makes sense" or "I'm with you", so that the other person has a back channel even without your face.

It also helps to know the person's usual voice. A colleague you only ever hear on audio still has a baseline: their normal pace, their usual pauses, their laugh. Changes from that baseline are as informative as changes in a face.

questions.q: Do some people find video calls more tiring than others?
questions.a:
Yes. Fauville, Bailenson and colleagues found that women, on average, reported more video call fatigue than men, and that this was linked partly to mirror anxiety, the strain of seeing their own face, and to feeling physically trapped in front of the camera. People who are anxious, neurodivergent, in poor health or in difficult home settings may also find calls harder. This is one reason to avoid assuming that everyone can cope with long days of video, and to design calls with breaks, optional cameras and audio-only options.

It also helps to ask people what works for them. Some people find a short break with the camera off halfway through a long call makes a large difference, and they may not ask for it unless invited.

It also helps to know that the effect is an average, and that individuals vary a great deal. Asking people what works for them is better than assuming.

questions.q: How long should a video meeting be?
questions.a:
Shorter than most are. Many meetings fill an hour because the calendar offers an hour, when twenty or thirty minutes would do. Shorter meetings, with breaks between them, reduce fatigue and keep attention higher. A simple habit is to end meetings five or ten minutes before the hour or half hour, so that people have time to stand up, move and look away from a screen before the next one. For one-to-one conversations where faces add little, a phone call, perhaps while walking, can be better than any video meeting.

It also helps to keep large group calls for broadcasting information, and to use smaller calls or messages for discussion. A grid of twenty faces is a poor setting for real conversation.

It also helps to ask whether a meeting is needed at all. A short written update, a shared document or a quick message can often do the job of a call, and save everyone half an hour in front of a camera.

watch.title: Children crash a live TV interview
watch.notice: The famous live interview interrupted by a professor's children. Notice how he tries to hold his on-camera posture while chaos unfolds behind him, and how much of a video-call body is about the frame.

reviewPrompt: This week, raise your camera to eye level, hide your self-view, and leave a longer pause than feels natural before moving on in any call you chair.
